183.title: At-Tin: the fig and the olive
183.hook: by the fig, the olive, Sinai and the safe city, the human was made in the best stature (Surah 95)
183.howItsDone: At-Tin is recited in the prayers, and the Prophet recited it in the evening prayer while traveling; its verse on the best stature is often quoted in teaching about human dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Alaq, and the man who tried to stop a servant from praying. Your line was bow and draw near.

A companion of the Prophet named al-Bara' remembered one night on a journey. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ led the evening prayer and recited a short surah that starts with fruit: by the fig and the olive. Al-Bara' said, and it's recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, that he had never heard anyone with a more beautiful voice or recitation. Of all the things he might have remembered from his time with the Prophet, he remembered a voice, at night, reciting about figs.
screen: `A NIGHT ON A JOURNEY.` → `BY THE FIG AND THE OLIVE.` → `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL VOICE.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-five opens with four oaths, in Pickthall's translation: By the fig and the olive, By Mount Sinai, And by this land made safe. Why fig and olive? Commentators give two answers, and hold both. The fruits themselves, gifts of the earth, sweet and nourishing. And the places they grow: some commentators link the fig and olive to the lands around Jerusalem, home to earlier prophets. Mount Sinai is where Musa received revelation, and this land made safe is Mecca, where the Prophet was. So some scholars read the oaths as a map of revelation: the lands of the prophets, Musa's mountain, Muhammad's city. Then the point of all four oaths: Surely We created man of the best stature. Ahsan taqwim: the finest form, the best proportion, body and mind and soul. That's the Qur'an's starting point about human beings: made well, beautifully, on purpose. Then a hard line: then We reduced him to the lowest of the low. Commentators read it several ways: old age and frailty, or the fall that comes when a person turns away. Except, it says, those who believe and do good. They have a reward that never ends. So the surah holds both: made in the best form, and able to fall far from it. The dignity is the beginning, not something you have to earn. What you do with it is the story.
screen: `FIG, OLIVE, SINAI, THE SAFE LAND.` · `A MAP OF REVELATION.` · `AHSAN TAQWIM — THE BEST STATURE.` · `THE LOWEST OF THE LOW, EXCEPT —` · then, large: `MADE IN THE BEST FORM.`

segments.voice: Hold a fig or an olive, or any fruit, and look at it closely, the color, the skin, how it's put together; then eat it slowly, and if you pray, say bismillah first and alhamdulillah after. If you don't have one, look at your own hand the same way: the joints, the lines, how it moves.
At-Tin. The fig, the first oath of Surah ninety-five, which says the human was made in the best stature. Today's word.
Your line: made in the best form. That goes for the face in the mirror, and for every other face too. Until tomorrow.

184.title: Ash-Sharh: the opened chest
184.hook: did We not expand your chest and lift your burden (94:1–3)
184.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Musa's supplication from Surah Ta-Ha, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before exams, speeches and difficult tasks, and Surah ash-Sharh is often recited in times of stress.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Tin, the fig and the olive, and the human made in the best stature. Your line was made in the best form.

Stress has an address, and often it's the chest. It gets tight. Breathing gets shallow. My chest is heavy, people say. I've got a weight on me. And when it lifts, when the news is good, when the fight is over, the first thing people do is take a long, full breath. Today's surah is about exactly that feeling. It's spoken to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in hard years in Mecca, and it starts with a question about his chest.
screen: `STRESS LIVES IN THE CHEST.` → `A WEIGHT ON ME.` → `THEN, A LONG BREATH.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate, And eased thee of the burden Which weighed down thy back. Sharh means opening, expanding, making wide. In Arabic, a narrow chest is anxiety, grief, feeling trapped. An opened chest is relief, calm, room to breathe, and room to understand and accept. The surah asks, as if reminding a friend: didn't We open your chest? Didn't We take off the weight that was breaking your back? It's spoken in the past tense: look, it already happened. Commentators give the opening two senses. One is inward: calm, guidance and the strength to carry the revelation. The other, some connect with a report in Sahih Muslim: when the Prophet was a young boy, playing with other children, Jibril came, opened his chest, washed his heart with Zamzam water, and closed it again. Then: and We raised your name, your remembrance. Commentators point to the call to prayer, where his name is said after Allah's. There's another opened chest in the Qur'an. Musa, sent to face Pharaoh, prays: my Lord, expand my chest for me, and ease my task. You'll hear his words, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before an exam, a hard talk, a speech. In the Qur'an, a heavy chest can be opened, and a burden can be lifted.

segments.voice: Sit up, put one hand on your chest, and breathe in slowly, feeling it rise and widen; breathe out and let your shoulders drop. If something heavy is sitting there, name it, and let the next out-breath carry some of it away. If you pray, you can say Musa's words: rabbi ishrah li sadri.
Ash-Sharh. The opening, the widening of the chest; the name of Surah ninety-four. Today's word.
Your line: the burden lifts. Some weights already have. Day one hundred eighty-four, done.

185.title: Ash-Sharh: with hardship, ease
185.hook: with hardship comes ease, said twice (94:5–6)
185.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 94:5–6, inna ma'a al-'usri yusra, to comfort each other in illness, loss and hard times, and the verse is common in calligraphy in homes and on cards.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh, the opened chest and the lifted burden. Your line was the burden lifts.

Some sentences get written on hospital whiteboards, taped above desks during exam season, texted at three in the morning to a friend whose marriage just ended. One short Qur'anic line turns up in places like these: in Arabic calligraphy on living-room walls, on phone lock screens, on the last page of a student's notebook. It's said twice in a row, and the way it's worded is more hopeful than a quick reading suggests.
screen: `ON WHITEBOARDS, DESKS, LOCK SCREENS.` → `SAID TWICE IN A ROW.` → `MORE HOPEFUL THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: After the opened chest, the lifted burden and the raised name, the surah says, in Pickthall's translation: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice the first small word: ma'a, with. Not after hardship. With it. The ease isn't only waiting at the end of the hard thing; it's already inside it, traveling alongside. Even a hard stretch often has something that holds a person up: a friend who shows up, a night of good sleep, a moment of laughter at the hospital. Now the grammar, which classical commentators dwelt on. In Arabic, hardship is al-'usr, with the word the: the hardship, the same one both times. But ease is yusr, without the: an ease, and then another ease. The same hardship, said twice, meets two different eases. A saying reported from early Muslims puts it this way: one hardship will never overcome two eases. Scholars discuss how firmly that saying traces back, but commentators still teach the reading of the grammar. Then the surah ends with what to do: when you're free of one task, keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing. Not sit and wait for ease. Keep going, toward Him. Tradition places this surah in the hard years in Mecca, when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had few followers and the pressure was heavy. It didn't promise that the hardship would vanish. It promised company for it.

Ash-Sharh. The opened chest, and the surah that says twice: with hardship comes ease. Today's word.

186.title: Ad-Duha: the morning
186.hook: your Lord has not left you, and what comes after is better (93:1–5)
186.tomorrow: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker
186.howItsDone: Many Muslims turn to Surah ad-Duha in times of sadness or waiting; the mid-morning voluntary prayer, salat ad-duha, shares its name with the surah's first word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh again, and the line said twice. Your line was with hardship, ease.

You text someone you love, and they don't answer. An hour. A day. A week. And your mind fills the silence: they're angry, they're done with me, I did something wrong. Silence is where the worst stories get written. Something like that happened to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In the early years of revelation, the verses stopped coming. Days passed, then more. People around him noticed, and some were cruel about it. The silence ended with this surah, and its first word is light.
screen: `THE TEXT THAT ISN'T ANSWERED.` → `SILENCE WRITES THE WORST STORIES.` → `THE REVELATION PAUSED.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records that the Prophet fell ill and didn't rise for prayer at night for a few nights, and a woman taunted him that his companion, meaning the one who brought the revelation, had abandoned him. Reports differ on the length of the pause and on who said what. They share the silence, and the sting. Then came Surah ninety-three. In Pickthall's translation: By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee, And verily the latter portion will be better for thee than the former, And verily thy Lord will give unto thee so that thou wilt be content. Duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is warm. Two oaths: the bright morning and the still night. In the surah, both belong to the same Lord. The night didn't mean the morning was gone; it was just night. Then the direct answer to the fear: your Lord has not left you, and He is not angry with you. Two sentences, answering exactly the two worst stories silence tells. Then a promise: the later will be better for you than the earlier. Commentators read it two ways: the rest of his life better than its beginning, and the next life better than this one. And a last line: your Lord will give you until you are content. Not a lecture. Something closer to a hand on the shoulder.
screen: `THE SILENCE, AND THE TAUNT.` · `BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.` · `NOT FORSAKEN, NOT HATED.` · `THE LATTER BETTER THAN THE FORMER.` · then, large: `THE LATER IS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Think of a silence in your life right now, something you're waiting on, and notice the story your mind is writing into it. Then set that story down, picture the morning after a long night, the light getting warm, and hold one hope that begins: later, I hope.
Ad-Duha. The bright morning, the name of Surah ninety-three, which says: your Lord has not left you, and the later is better. Today's word.
Your line: the later is better. Even a long silence can end in morning. See you tomorrow.

187.title: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker
187.hook: did He not find you an orphan and shelter you, so don't be harsh with orphans or turn askers away (93:6–10)
187.howItsDone: Care for orphans holds a special place in Muslim practice, from sponsoring orphans to supporting orphanages, and many Muslims recall 93:9–10 when someone asks them for help or a question.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ad-Duha, the morning after the silence. Your line was the later is better.

Ask someone who grew up without much why they notice certain people, and the answer is often short: I remember what it was like. The one who went to school hungry notices the kid with no lunch. The one who was new in the country notices the family that doesn't speak the language yet. Memory turns into attention. The second half of Surah ad-Duha asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to remember where he came from, and then tells him what to do with the memory.
screen: `I REMEMBER WHAT IT WAS LIKE.` → `MEMORY TURNS INTO ATTENTION.` → `WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The surah asks three questions, in Pickthall's translation: Did He not find thee an orphan and protect thee? Did He not find thee wandering and direct thee? Did He not find thee destitute and enrich thee? The early biographies fill in each line. His father died before he was born. His mother, they say, died when he was about six, and his grandfather, who took him in, two years later. Then his uncle Abu Talib raised him. An orphan three times over, and each time, someone sheltered him. Wandering, commentators say, means searching, not yet guided, before revelation came. Destitute: he was poor, and commentators often connect his later means to his marriage to Khadijah and his work in trade. Then the surah turns those memories into two instructions: Therefor the orphan oppress not, Therefor the beggar drive not away. The Arabic for the beggar is as-sa'il, the one who asks. Some commentators read it as covering both: the one who asks for money or food, and the one who asks a question, who comes to learn. Don't brush off either one, or sigh at them, or make them feel small for asking. The Prophet said, in a hadith in Bukhari, holding up two fingers side by side: I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. You were sheltered, so shelter. You were guided, so answer the one who asks.
screen: `AN ORPHAN, AND SHELTERED.` · `WANDERING, AND GUIDED.` · `AS-SA'IL — THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `LIKE THESE TWO FINGERS.` · then, large: `DON'T TURN THE ASKER AWAY.`

segments.voice: Remember one time you needed something and someone gave it: a meal, a ride, an answer, a place to stay. Picture their face, and let the memory of being helped come back. Then decide how you'll meet the next person who asks: a yes if you can, a kind answer if you can't, and no sigh.
Ad-Duha. The bright morning, and the surah that says: you were an orphan and were sheltered, so don't turn the asker away. Today's word.
Your line: don't turn the asker away. The memory of need is meant to become kindness. One hundred eighty-seven days now.

188.title: Ad-Duha: speak of the blessings
188.hook: and as for the favor of your Lord, speak of it (93:11)
188.howItsDone: Many Muslims make a habit of naming blessings aloud, answering how are you with alhamdulillah and thanking the people through whom good came, while taking care that speaking of a gift doesn't become boasting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ad-Duha, the orphan and the one who asks. Your line was don't turn the asker away.

How's it going? The answer tends to come in one of two settings. Complain, because complaining is safe and everyone can join in. Or say fine and move on, because saying something went well feels like bragging, or like tempting fate. So the good things go unsaid: the job that worked out, the friend who showed up, the morning the pain was a little less. Ad-Duha, the surah of the morning light, ends on a line that pushes against that habit. After reminding the Prophet of everything he was given, the last word isn't keep quiet. It's the opposite.
screen: `COMPLAIN, OR SAY FINE.` → `THE GOOD THINGS GO UNSAID.` → `THE LAST LINE OF AD-DUHA.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-three has eleven verses, and the last three are instructions. The orphan: don't be harsh with him. The one who asks: don't drive him away. Then verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse. The Arabic is short: fa-haddith. Speak of it. Tell it. The same root gives the word hadith, a report, a thing told. So the surah that began with the morning light, and the promise that the later would be better, ends by asking for the good to be told out loud. Commentators read the bounty in more than one way. Some say it means the revelation itself: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was being told to share the revelation he had been given. Others read it more widely: every favor, from guidance to food to health, is something to acknowledge rather than hide. Some hold both at once. Scholars are careful to separate this from showing off. A gift told as a gift points past you to where it came from; a boast points back at you. Often the difference is one word: I did this, or this was given to me. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi adds a human side: whoever does not thank people has not thanked God. So speaking of the bounty isn't only upward. It's also telling the teacher, the parent, the stranger at the bus stop, that what they gave you landed. The orphan, the asker, the blessing: three verses, one direction. Open hands and an open mouth.
screen: `THREE INSTRUCTIONS TO END THE SURAH.` · `FA-HADDITH — SPEAK OF IT.` · `A GIFT TOLD, NOT A BOAST.` · `THANK PEOPLE TOO.` · then, large: `SPEAK OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing from this week, something given, not something you earned, and hold it until you see it clearly. Then think of one person you could tell, in a single sentence: this happened, and I'm grateful. If you pray, you can add alhamdulillah.
Ad-Duha. The morning light, Surah ninety-three, which closes with speak of the bounty of your Lord. Today's word.

189.title: Al-Layl: the night
189.hook: by the night and the day, your strivings are different (Surah 92)
189.howItsDone: Al-Layl is one of the short surahs often learned by heart and recited in the prayer; its opening oaths, by the night and the day, are often read as a reminder that every person's effort is heading somewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last line of Ad-Duha, the good told out loud. Your line was speak of the gift.

Eleven at night, one quiet street, two people under the same streetlight. One is driving home from a double shift so her kids can eat. The other is out to do something he hopes nobody finds out about. From a satellite, they look identical: two dots moving in the dark. The night covers them both. What's different is where each one is going, and why. The surah just before Ad-Duha, Al-Layl, the night, opens on that same picture: night and day, male and female, and then a sentence that could be written about any street, any office, any family group chat.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, THE SAME DARK STREET.` → `THE NIGHT COVERS THEM BOTH.` → `AL-LAYL, THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-two begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the night enshrouding. The night that covers, that wraps things so you can't see them. Then by the day when it shines, and by the One who created the male and the female. Three oaths, all pairs: dark and light, one and the other. Then the point they lead to, verse four, in Pickthall's words: Lo! your effort is dispersed. Scattered, going in different directions. The Arabic word for effort is sa'y, effort with your feet in it, hurrying toward something. Pilgrims use the same word, sa'y, for the walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa during Hajj, retracing Hajar's run for water. And shatta, the word describing the effort, means scattered, as different from each other as night from day. So: everyone is under the same sky, but the efforts aren't the same. Some run toward what's good. Some run away from it. The night hides the difference for a while. It doesn't erase it. Notice what the surah doesn't say: not that effort is wasted, or that effort is bad. Only that effort has a direction. The next verses, tomorrow's, name the two directions; today is only the question. It's the end of a week, too: At-Tin, made in the best form; Ash-Sharh, the chest opened and hardship paired with ease; Ad-Duha, the morning, the orphan and the gift told out loud. Now the night, and the question under all of them: where is the effort going?
screen: `THREE OATHS, ALL IN PAIRS.` · `SA'Y — STRIVING, EFFORT WITH FEET.` · `SHATTA — SCATTERED, NOT THE SAME.` · `EFFORT HAS A DIRECTION.` · then, large: `EFFORTS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Look back over yesterday as if from above, like that satellite, and ask where your effort actually went, not where you meant it to go: the phone, the work, a person, a worry. Don't judge it. Just notice the direction, the way you'd notice which way a river runs.
